name: Gradient Descent
statement: Minimize a function by repeatedly stepping downhill in the direction of steepest descent.
statementAccent: stepping downhill in the direction of steepest descent
meaning: Gradient descent is a first-order iterative optimization algorithm for finding a local minimum of a differentiable function. The idea is simple: to minimize a function, one repeatedly takes steps in the direction of the negative gradient at the current point, because the gradient points in the direction of steepest increase, so its negative points in the direction of steepest decrease, or steepest descent. The update rule is that the next point equals the current point minus the learning rate times the gradient of the function at the current point. Here the gradient is the vector of partial derivatives, and the learning rate, often written as eta, is a positive scalar, also called the step size, that controls how large each step is. The steps are repeated until the process converges, when the gradient is near zero or the changes become small. The learning rate is crucial: too small a rate makes convergence slow, while too large a rate can cause the steps to overshoot the minimum and diverge or oscillate. For convex functions, gradient descent converges to the global minimum with a suitable step size, but for non-convex functions, such as the loss surfaces of neural networks, it may converge only to a local minimum or slow near a saddle point. The method is generally attributed to Augustin-Louis Cauchy, who proposed it in 1847. Gradient descent, especially its stochastic variants, is the workhorse optimizer of modern machine learning and deep learning.
mechanism: Gradient descent minimizes a differentiable function by following the local slope downhill in small repeated steps. At any point, the gradient of the function, the vector of its partial derivatives, points in the direction in which the function increases most steeply; its negative therefore points in the direction of steepest decrease. Gradient descent uses this directly: from a current estimate, it computes the gradient there and moves a short distance in the opposite direction, obtaining a new estimate, then repeats. Formally, the next point is the current point minus the learning rate times the gradient at the current point, and this iteration continues until the gradient is essentially zero, signalling a stationary point, or until successive changes are negligible. The learning rate governs the size of each step and must be chosen with care: if it is too small, progress is slow and many iterations are needed; if it is too large, a step can jump past the minimum, and the sequence may oscillate or diverge rather than settle. The behaviour also depends on the shape of the function. When the function is convex, every local minimum is the global minimum, and gradient descent with an appropriate step size converges to that global optimum; when the function is non-convex, as with the highly complex loss surfaces of deep neural networks, gradient descent finds only a local minimum and can slow dramatically near saddle points, though in practice this often suffices. In machine learning, the function being minimized is a loss measuring how badly a model fits its data, and the gradients are supplied by backpropagation; because computing the exact gradient over a whole dataset is expensive, practitioners use stochastic gradient descent, which estimates the gradient from one or a few random examples per step, trading noise for speed, along with mini-batch, momentum, and adaptive variants such as AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam.

variants.text: On convex functions gradient descent reaches the global minimum; on non-convex ones it may find only a local minimum or a saddle point.

variants.name: Adaptive optimizers
variants.text: Momentum, AdaGrad, RMSProp, and Adam extend gradient descent with momentum and per-parameter learning rates.

whyItMatters: Gradient descent is one of the most important optimization algorithms in science and engineering, and it is the engine that trains almost all of modern machine learning. Optimization, finding the inputs that minimize or maximize some function, lies at the heart of countless problems, and gradient descent offers a general, remarkably simple recipe: follow the slope downhill. Its significance has exploded with deep learning, where training a model means minimizing a loss function over enormous numbers of parameters, and gradient descent, in its stochastic and adaptive forms and fed by gradients from backpropagation, is what makes this possible; every large neural network, from image recognizers to language models, is trained by some variant of gradient descent. The method's clarity also makes it a foundational teaching example, illustrating gradients, iteration, learning rates, convergence, and the difference between convex and non-convex optimization, and it seeds a whole family of more sophisticated optimizers like Momentum and Adam. Its lineage is long, generally traced to Cauchy in 1847, yet its central role is thoroughly modern, and the practical craft of setting learning rates and choosing variants is a daily concern of machine-learning practitioners everywhere. As the method that minimizes a function by repeatedly stepping downhill in the direction of steepest descent, gradient descent is a cornerstone of optimization and artificial intelligence.

limits: Gradient descent is general and powerful but has real limits that reward care. On non-convex functions, which include the loss surfaces of deep neural networks, it is guaranteed only to reach a local minimum, not the global one, and it can stall near saddle points or in flat regions; convergence to the global optimum is assured only for convex functions with a suitable step size. Its performance hinges on the learning rate, which is not automatically known: too small and it crawls, too large and it overshoots or diverges, and choosing or scheduling it well is a genuine practical difficulty, partly addressed by adaptive methods. Gradient descent also requires the function to be differentiable, so that a gradient exists, and it uses only first-order information, so it can be slow on ill-conditioned problems where second-order or momentum methods do better. The stochastic variants trade exactness for speed by estimating the gradient from samples, which introduces noise. Some historical details reward care: the method is generally attributed to Cauchy in 1847, with related work by Hadamard and later Haskell Curry in 1944, and stochastic gradient descent and optimizers like Adam are its modern descendants. So gradient descent robustly minimizes differentiable functions by stepping downhill, understood as finding local rather than global minima in general and depending critically on the learning rate.
misreadings: Gradient descent does not, in general, find the global minimum; on non-convex functions it reaches only a local minimum or a saddle point. It is not parameter-free, since the learning rate must be chosen and badly set rates diverge. And it needs a differentiable function and uses only first-order information, so treating it as a global optimizer, as automatic, or as applicable to any function, misreads it.
origin: The first-order iterative optimization method generally attributed to Augustin-Louis Cauchy in 1847, which minimizes a differentiable function by repeatedly stepping in the direction of the negative gradient.
